title: How to memorialize client meetings on Mac: a faster routine for lawyers in 2026
metaTitle: How to Memorialize Client Meetings on Mac for Lawyers (2026)
description: Write a client meeting memo in one sitting, with a fixed layout, voice dictation and a same-day routine. Practical steps for Mac lawyers in 2026.
secondaryKeywords: dictate client meeting notes on Mac
intro: To memorialize a client meeting, write a short memo while the call is still fresh. Record the date, who attended, what the client told you, what you advised, and who does what next. Then file it in the matter record, where your team will look for it.
tldr: Write the memo the same day, while the call is still fresh in your head.
Use one fixed layout with the same headings every time, saved once as a Word template.
Dictate the first draft with Apple Dictation or Word's Dictate, then check every name, date and figure.
Record facts, decisions and instructions. Leave out the transcript and your commentary.
Follow your firm's rules on client data before you use dictation or any AI tool.

blocks.text: How to memorialize client meetings: a memo layout you can reuse

A memo is a record that someone else can act on. It is not a transcript of the call. Your goal is simple. A supervising attorney, a paralegal or your future self should be able to tell what was said, what was decided and what is still open. Use the same layout every time. Then you stop deciding what to include, and the writing goes faster.

rows: Date, matter name or number, client, everyone present, and anyone absent who should have been there
Why the call happened, in one sentence, such as a status check on a lease dispute
Facts, deadlines and concerns, in the client's own words where the wording matters
Your advice, the options you named, and any risks you flagged
What the client chose, and any instruction they gave you to act on
Who does what by when, plus questions you still need answered
blocks.caption: The sections of a client meeting memo, in order

blocks.text: The header does more work than people expect. Write down who attended, and who did not but should have. If the client brought an assistant, a relative or an accountant, note that too. Those details can affect privilege, so ask your supervising attorney how your firm handles them rather than guessing. Use the matter name in the format your firm uses, so the memo sorts with everything else.
Write the memo in this order, while the call is still fresh.

items: Open the saved template before the call ends, or straight after. Do not start from a blank page.
Fill in the header first, including the full name of everyone who spoke.
Write the purpose and the client's facts as short bullets. Skip the greeting and the small talk.
Record your advice in plain words. Note any option the client rejected, and why, if they said.
Add each decision and action item with a named owner and a date.
Read it once against your notes, then send it to the people who need it.

blocks.text: A worked example: a lease call written up the same day

Say a client calls about a late rent payment on a shared office lease. The landlord has sent a notice. The client wants to know whether to pay now or wait. This example is invented. Use it as a shape, not as advice for a real matter.

items: Purpose: Status call on the landlord's late payment notice, received the week before the call.
What the client told us: The rent went to the bank, not the landlord. The client has the transfer record and will forward it today.
What we advised: Do not pay the disputed amount until we review the notice. Respond in writing before the cure period in the lease ends.
Decisions: The client wants to keep the lease. The client will send the transfer record.
Action items: Associate reviews the notice and the late-fee clause by end of day Friday. Paralegal calendars the cure deadline.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing. There is no transcript, no small talk and no commentary about the other side. Someone who was not on the call can act on this memo without calling you. That is the test for a good one.
Dictate client meeting notes instead of typing them

Speech is faster than typing for short text, but it is not cleaner. A 2016 study of mobile text entry found speech 2.93 times faster than a keyboard for English, at 153 words per minute against 52. The same study found more errors left in the final text with speech, at 1.30 percent against 0.79 percent. Speak the draft, then fix it by eye.

On a Mac, start with Apple's Dictation. Open System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation and turn it on. Then start it from Edit > Start Dictation, or press the Microphone key. Apple's guide says Dictation stops after 30 seconds without speech. Pause and restart it when you need to, rather than waiting on it.

Word has its own option. In Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac, go to Home > Dictate, or press Option+F1. Word 2024 and Word 2021 for Mac also have it. Dictate needs a Microsoft 365 subscription and a reliable internet connection. Microsoft says it sends your speech to Microsoft to make text, and that it does not store the audio or the transcribed text. Confirm with your firm that this is allowed for client matters.
Check the draft against your notes, line by line

Dictated drafts fail in predictable places. Names come out wrong. Dates shift. A dollar figure loses a zero, or a per month figure becomes a per year figure. Read the draft once with your call notes beside it. Treat every name, number and date as unverified until you match it.

items: Check each proper name against your intake sheet, including the landlord's exact company name.
Check each date and deadline against the calendar entry, not against memory.
Check each figure and its unit, such as per month or per year.
Delete any legal conclusion you did not reach on the call. Keep it as a question instead.
Remove filler you dictated while thinking, such as 'um' or 'so anyway'.

blocks.text: Do this pass right after you dictate, while the call is still clear. A week later the memo reads like a stranger's, and you will miss the gaps. If you find a fact you cannot confirm, mark it as open in the memo. Do not guess it into a clean sentence.
Where the memo goes and who needs a copy

A memo that sits on your desktop helps nobody. File it in the matter record your firm uses, under the matter name, so the next person finds it without asking you. If your firm uses Outlook, keep the follow-up email linked to the same matter, so the email thread and the record tell the same story. For filing habits in Outlook, see [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook).

Build the template once and reuse it. In Word, type the headings into a blank document and set up the layout. Then choose File > Save As and pick Word Template (.dotx) as the format. Next time, open a new document from that template. If you draft in Word all day, [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word) covers review steps that pair well with a memo.

Give the file a name that sorts well. A pattern such as client name, date and call type works in most folder systems. Keep one convention across the team, and say it out loud at the start of each matter. A consistent name saves time every time someone searches.
Hallway talks, group calls and unplanned calls

Not every client contact is a scheduled meeting. A hallway question or a call from a client's accountant can matter as much as a formal meeting. Write a short memo for it too, and label it as informal. Note what you knew, what you did not know, and whether you promised anything.

Group calls need more care. List every participant and their role. If someone joined from outside your firm, note who they are and who invited them. Confidential information shared with a third party can raise privilege questions. Ask your supervising attorney before the memo leaves the firm.

Recorded calls need a separate check. Recording laws vary by state, and some states require every party to agree before a call is recorded. Confirm the rules with your firm before you press record, and keep any consent in the matter file.
Privacy and firm rules before you use any tool

Client information is confidential. The rules that cover it come from your employer, your state bar and your client agreements. Follow your firm's policy on which tools may touch client data. If the policy is unclear, ask before you dictate a client name into anything. A quick question to a supervisor costs less than a disclosure problem.

Each tool handles audio differently, so read each policy. Microsoft says Dictate sends speech to Microsoft to make text, and does not store the audio or the text. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm still decides what is allowed.
What research says about AI and lawyer speed

AI can speed up legal work, but the quality results are mixed. In a randomized trial with law students at Minnesota, Michigan and Ogletree Deakins, the authors report productivity gains of 34 to 140 percent. The tools included o1-preview and Vincent AI. The study described accuracy as mixed, and it gave no accuracy figures.

An earlier study in the Minnesota Law Review assigned law students to tasks with or without GPT-4. GPT-4 brought large and consistent gains in speed. Quality gains were slight and uneven. The practical lesson is to bank the speed on the draft, then spend the saved time checking it.
A field study of 758 BCG consultants found 25.1 percent faster completion with AI. Those were consulting tasks, not legal work. Read it as a sign of direction, not a forecast for your practice.
Note-taking tools that join calls: costs and questions to ask

Some tools join or listen to your meetings for you. Granola says its plans are bot-free and capture device audio. Its Business plan lists $14 per user per month, with unlimited meeting history. Check Granola's pricing page for current terms, because prices change.

Clio Notes is a free, open-source Mac app. Its site says it transcribes locally by default, using whisper.cpp, and records system audio plus your microphone. It also offers a Pro plan at $4.99 per month or $30 per year. It is unrelated to Clio's practice management software. The site also says AI summaries can go to third-party providers unless you run a local model, so read that part closely.

VXT Meet is built for law firms. It says it saves notes into legal software, lists Clio among its integrations, and says time is recorded automatically from conversations. The page lists no prices. It does not settle questions about bots or the accuracy of time entries. Ask the vendor those questions in writing before a pilot.
Mistakes that make the memo longer

items: Writing a transcript. Nobody reads a transcript after a call. Keep the facts and the decisions.
Waiting until the end of the week. Memory fades, and the memo grows as you rebuild the call.
Mixing your advice with your commentary on the other side. Keep them in separate sections.
Pasting client names into a tool your firm has not approved. Check the policy first.
Starting from a blank page each time. Open the saved template instead.
Leaving action items without an owner. A task with no name on it stays open.

blocks.text: Start the routine this week

Pick one active matter and run the routine on every call for the next few weeks. Track how long each memo takes, and note the section where you stall. The pattern shows up fast. Lazur has a free trial with no credit card, and dictation is unlimited on its paid plans. Compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing), or [download](/download) the app to try it on your Mac.

faq.question: Do I need to write a memo after every client call?
faq.answer: Not every call needs a memo. Any call that gives advice, sets a deadline, changes the scope of work or raises a risk should have one. Ask your supervising attorney what your firm expects, and follow that rule.

faq.question: How long should a client meeting memo be?
faq.answer: Long enough that a colleague who was not on the call can act on it without asking you. Most memos fit on one page. If yours runs longer, cut the transcript-style detail first and keep the decisions.

faq.question: Is a client meeting memo the same as a time entry?
faq.answer: No. A time entry records the time you spent for billing. The memo records what happened on the call. Check how your firm handles each one, and keep them separate.

faq.question: Can I dictate a client memo with Apple Dictation?
faq.answer: Yes, after you turn it on in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Apple says Dictation stops after 30 seconds without speech. Confirm with your firm whether dictating client details is allowed before you start.

faq.question: Does Lazur record my client calls?
faq.answer: Lazur does not listen in the background. It listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Check your firm's policy before you use any AI tool on client matters.

faq.question: Is the memo privileged?
faq.answer: Privilege depends on the facts, the people present and the purpose of the communication. A memo can help show what was discussed, but the label alone does not protect it. Ask your supervising attorney before you share the memo outside the firm.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur is for macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.

problem: client meeting memos eating post-call time

costs.title: Evenings and weekends
costs.text: A memo that waits until after hours becomes a second shift. The ABA and CoLAP study of about 37,000 lawyers found 47 percent screened high for burnout, and 16 percent severe. One memo will not cause that. Still, it is a daily load you can shrink.

costs.title: Burnout you feel during the day
costs.text: Bloomberg Law's survey of more than 1,000 legal professionals in the second half of 2024 found attorneys felt burned out 42 percent of the time. Mid- and senior-level associates reported 51 percent. Admin work that follows you home adds to that feeling.

costs.title: Billable time you cannot bill
costs.text: When a memo is late, you rebuild the call from scraps, and that rebuilding is hard to bill. No public study measures how long post-call memos take, so track your own for a few weeks before you decide what it costs you.

costs.title: A thin record
costs.text: A vague or late memo weakens the record your team depends on. Colleagues cannot act on it, and a question months later may catch you without the detail. The cost shows up on the day someone needs the file.

costs.title: Pay in context, not a price tag
costs.text: The median annual wage for lawyers was $159,670 in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That is a salary figure, not a billing value. Use it as context for your time, not as a rate for memos.

causes.title: The next call starts before the last memo does
causes.text: Most calls run straight into the next task. The memo is the first thing pushed back. By the time you return to it, the details have blurred, and rebuilding them eats the time you meant to save.

causes.title: Every memo starts from a blank page
causes.text: Without a fixed layout, you decide what goes in each time. Those small decisions add up. You also tend to leave out a section, such as action items, when you are tired at the end of a long day.

causes.title: Full sentences take longer than bullets
causes.text: A memo written as prose asks you to think about grammar as well as content. Bullets carry the facts and decisions with less effort. Prose can come later, if the reader needs it.

causes.title: Call notes that only you can read
causes.text: Shorthand that makes sense during the call often means nothing a week later. Arrows, initials and half sentences fail once the client's name has faded from your memory.

causes.title: No owner for the follow-up
causes.text: A memo without a named owner for each action item stalls. Everyone assumes someone else will send the follow-up or make the call. The gap shows up only when a deadline passes.

causes.title: Memos split across three places
causes.text: Notes sit on paper, the draft sits in Word, and the final goes into an email thread. Finding the memo before you start the next task takes longer than it should.

fixes.title: Set a same-day rule for memos
fixes.text: Decide that every client call gets a memo the same day. Write the bullets straight after the call, while the wording is still in your head. A same-day memo stays short because you remember what mattered. A memo written a week later runs long.

fixes.title: Keep a few lines of notes during the call
fixes.text: Write short notes while the client talks. Put down who wants what, what they must do, and what you promised. Use plain words, not shorthand, because arrows and initials mean little a week later. A few lines are enough to rebuild the memo fast.

fixes.title: Recap decisions before you hang up
fixes.text: Repeat the decisions and action items at the end of the call. Ask the client whether you got it right. A spoken recap settles disagreements while everyone is still on the line, so the memo does not have to settle them later.

fixes.title: Dictate the bullets, then check them
fixes.text: Speak the first draft into Word or Pages with Dictation. Then check names, dates and figures against your notes. Speaking is faster than typing for short text. The cleanup step keeps that speed honest, so do not skip it.

fixes.title: Turn action items into reminders
fixes.text: Put each action item into Apple Reminders with a due date and the name of the person who owns it. A reminder is a second record of the task. The task stays visible even when the memo sits in a folder nobody opens.

fixes.title: Save repeated sentences as snippets
fixes.text: Many memos repeat the same sentences, such as scope limits or a standard caveat about timing. Save those once as snippets in Lazur and reuse them. Check the wording against the matter first, because a sentence that fits one matter may not fit another.

fixes.title: Block a memo slot on your calendar
fixes.text: Put a short memo block on your calendar before you log off for the day. Work through the open calls in order. A fixed slot stops memos from drifting into the next morning, and it makes the backlog easy to see.

fixes.title: Review your own pattern once a week
fixes.text: Once a week, look at the memos you wrote. Notice which section took longest and which section you skipped. Change one thing, such as the template or your note habit, and watch the next week. Small changes beat a big reset.

lazurHelps.say: Hold fn and dictate the memo into Word.
lazurHelps.result: Dictated text appears at the cursor in any app. You still read it back and fix the names and dates.

lazurHelps.say: Walk me through turning on Dictation in System Settings.
lazurHelps.result: Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not click for you.

lazurHelps.say: Where is the Dictate button in Word?
lazurHelps.result: Lazur draws a circle and a label around the Dictate button on the Home tab.

lazurHelps.say: What am I looking at on this screen?
lazurHelps.result: Lazur answers out loud about what is on screen, so you can check a message or setting before you act.

lazurHelps.say: Draft a short follow-up to the client from these notes.
lazurHelps.result: Lazur drafts the text. You check every name, date and piece of advice before it goes anywhere.

lazurHelps.say: Remind me to file the memo before I leave today.
lazurHelps.result: Adds a reminder in Apple Reminders. Lazur does not file the memo for you.

demo.context: Word, a memo open after a client call
demo.spoken: Client call on the late rent notice. Landlord wants payment by Friday. Client sends the transfer record today.
demo.output: Punctuated sentences typed at the cursor, with names from your personal dictionary spelled the way you taught them.
demo.result: You read the draft against your notes, fix any names or dates, then file it yourself. Lazur does not save the file for you.

plan.label: Call ends
plan.title: Say the recap out loud
plan.text: Before you hang up, repeat the decisions and action items back to the client. Ask them to confirm. Jot a few lines of notes in plain words while you talk, so you have something to rebuild from.

plan.label: Within the hour
plan.title: Dictate the bullets
plan.text: Open your saved Word template and dictate the first draft while the call is still clear. Stick to the template headings. Do not stop to polish every sentence.

plan.label: Same day
plan.title: Check and file
plan.text: Compare names, dates and figures against your notes. Remove any legal conclusion you did not reach on the call. File the memo in the matter record, then send the follow-up email.

plan.label: Next morning
plan.title: Set the action items
plan.text: Put each action item into Apple Reminders with the owner and due date. Confirm the owner has the memo. Raise any open question on the matter before the next call.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Review your own pattern
plan.text: Look at the memos you wrote this week. Note which section took longest and which one you skipped. Change the template or your note habit before the next week starts.
